name: Mao
description: Mao is a unique card game known for its extreme secrecy and metagame elements. It is the most famous of the 'secret rule' games, where the only rule that may be explained to a new player is: 'The rules of Mao cannot be told.' New players must learn the rules through trial and error, as they are penalized (by drawing cards) for every infraction. Each winner of a round also gets to create a new secret rule for the next round, meaning the game evolves indefinitely.

history.origins: Its exact origin is shrouded in mystery, intentional or otherwise. It appeared in various US university campuses in the 1960s and 70s.
timeline: 1960s: Mao emerges as an underground 'cult' game in academic circles.
1980s: Variations appear with names like 'Mau' or 'The Game of the Great Helmsman'.
Present: A staple of theater troupes, summer camps, and math/science olympiads.
2004: Standardized 'Public' Mao rules are occasionally published, much to the annoyance of purists.
history.cultural: Often associated with surrealist humor and a lighthearted disdain for authority.
history.evolution: The game's rules are deliberately kept unwritten to preserve the 'Rite of Passage' aspect for new players.

setup.deck: Two shuffled standard decks. All cards face down.
setup.dealing: Each player is dealt 7 cards. Players CANNOT look at their cards until the game officially starts.

rules.objective: Be the first to shed all cards. When you play your last card, you must yell 'Mao!'.
rules.gameplay: Play proceeds clockwise from the dealer's left. On your turn, play one card that matches the rank or suit of the top card on the play pile, or draw one card from the stock if you cannot play. Breaking a rule incurs a penalty card. First to empty their hand and call 'Mao' (or 'game over') wins. Rules vary by group and are often learned by trial and error.
keyRules: Match the top card on the play pile by rank or suit; or draw one from stock if unable.
Call Mao or game over when playing your last card.
One penalty card per rule breach; the person giving it states what was wrong without explaining the rule.
Rules vary by group and are learned by observation and trial and error.

strategy.basic: Don't be the first to act! Watch the veterans. If they say 'Have a nice Day' every time they play a 7, YOU should say it too. Most of Mao is pattern recognition.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Chairman' Trap: If you are the Chairman, use your power to confuse new players. Give penalties for 'Failure to be Awesome' or 'Breathing too loudly'. This forces players to think outside the literal mechanics of the cards.
strategy.advanced: Rule-Stacking: If you win, create a rule that is triggered by a common action. For example, 'Every time a Red 4 is played, the person who played it must stand up.' Combine this with existing rules to create complex sequences of required actions.
tips: Keep a straight face. If you laugh at a penalty, you might get another penalty for 'Illegal Joy'.
If you are stuck, call a 'Point of Order'. It's the only safe time to observe the table without cards in hand.
